title: Learning Theory
subtitle: How feedback, prediction and practice shape self-regulation
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating learning theory within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain learning theory without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in learning theory.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to learning theory.

sections.explainSimply: The learner receives information about a brain signal and gradually discovers ways to change the probability of reaching a target state.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Neurofeedback combines operant learning, skill acquisition, motivation, expectancy and repeated state practice. Non-specific factors can contribute to improvement.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Learning depends on contingency, salience, shaping, task difficulty, reinforcement timing and transfer beyond the training environment. Evidence of signal learning and evidence of symptom change are related but distinct.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A driving instructor who gives immediate dashboard feedback while the learner practises a controllable skill.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand learning theory to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A pleasant session is not proof that the intended neural feature was learned.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using learning theory predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: A pleasant session is not proof that the intended neural feature was learned. Evidence classification: established learning principles; theoretical neural transfer.
